pamphlet_excerpts: Short History of Fingerprinting: Give A Short History: Galton was able to scientifically prove what Herschel and Faulds already suspected: that fingerprints are permanent and unique to each individual (p. 13).
Short History of Fingerprinting Principle 2: Give A Short History Principle 2: According to Galton's calculations, the odds of two individual fingerprints being the same were 1 in 64 billion (p. 13).

Short History of Fingerprinting Principle 3: Give A Short History Principle 3: In 1891, Juan Vucetich, an Argentine police official, began the first fingerprint files based on Galton pattern types (p. 13).
Short History of Fingerprinting Principle 4: Give A Short History Principle 4: In 1892, Vucetich made the first criminal fingerprint identification (p. 13).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Short History of Fingerprinting): Step 1 (Give A Short History): The classification system was based on Galton's observations, as revised by Sir Edward Richard Henry (p. 13).

Step 2 (Short History of Fingerprinting): Step 2 (Give A Short History): In 1903, the New York State prison system became the first agency in the United States to regularly use fingerprints to identify criminals (p. 13).
Step 3 (Short History of Fingerprinting): Step 3 (Give A Short History): The Leavenworth bureau became the first to operate on more than a local basis (p. 13).

Step 4 (Short History of Fingerprinting): Step 4 (Give A Short History): It gradually began to offer a free fingerprint exchange service among a growing list of participating lawenforcement officers (p. 13).

options: A. Friction ridge arrangements are unique to each individual (even identical twins) and remain unchanged in pattern from before birth until decomposition; the three main pattern families are loops, whorls, and arches.
B. Fingerprints change completely every seven years as a person ages; the three main pattern families are squares, triangles, and spirals.
C. Only the thumb has friction ridges while the other four fingers are smooth; patterns are classified by skin temperature and ink color.
D. Identical twins share identical fingerprints on all ten digits; the three pattern families are epidermal, dermal, and subcutaneous.

pamphlet_excerpts: Counselor You Can Identify: Your counselor you can identify: Fingerprints are classified into three basic types, loops, arches, and whorls, based on the patterns made by the ridges that cover the skin (p. 18).
Counselor You Can Identify Principle 2: Your counselor you can identify Principle 2: Learning to recognize these general patterns and their subcategories is not hard (p. 18).

Counselor You Can Identify Principle 3: Your counselor you can identify Principle 3: Study the examples shown in this pamphlet, then complete the worksheet found on page 38 to show your counselor you can identify the three basic types (p. 18).
Counselor You Can Identify Principle 4: Your counselor you can identify Principle 4: Also identify the pattern types of your own fingerprints (p. 18).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Counselor You Can Identify): Step 1 (Your counselor you can identify): In the loop pattern, the ridges begin on one side of the finger, curve or turn back sharply, and end on the same side (p. 18).
Step 2 (Counselor You Can Identify): Step 2 (Your counselor you can identify): The loop may slope or "lean" toward either the thumb or the little finger (p. 18).

Step 3 (Counselor You Can Identify): Step 3 (Your counselor you can identify): If you can identify the two bones in your forearm, the radius and ulna, then you can remember the two subcategoriesof loops (p. 18).

Step 4 (Counselor You Can Identify): Step 4 (Your counselor you can identify): The ridges of a radial loop begin and end on the same side of the hand as the thumb (or the radius, the bone that is on the inside of the arm) (p. 18).
